activities.anchor: Keep the distinction that organises everything
activities.caption: drag the divider — noise versus distribution
activities.name: ccWeatherCompare

config.prompt: The distinction that organises the whole page — drag the divider:

before.label: weather
before.text: What happens today: Tuesday's frost, this week's storm. A single draw from the distribution — noise, and proof of nothing in either direction.

after.label: climate
after.text: The statistics of decades — the distribution itself. Only the statistics have changed: record highs now outnumber record lows roughly two to one in the US, and a wavier jet stream can even deliver colder-looking episodes.

config.why: Cold snaps disprove nothing and warm snaps prove nothing on their own — judge the statistics, not Tuesday's frost.

activities.anchor: The evidence stacks four independent lines
activities.caption: file each observation under its evidence line
activities.name: ccEvidenceBuckets

config.prompt: Which line of evidence carries each observation? File them:

items.label: 2024: the warmest single year yet measured, near 1.55 °C above pre-industrial
the decade to 2020 about 1.1 °C warmer than 1850–1900
an 800,000-year record with CO₂ swinging between 172 and 300 ppm
Arctic September sea ice shrinking 12–13% per decade since 1979
oceans absorbing over 90% of the excess heat, warming top to bottom
London's frost fairs on a frozen Thames, a regular event 1607–1814
grape harvest dates and ship logs

config.why: Four independent lines converge — and today's 424 ppm stands far outside the ice-core envelope of 172–300 ppm, the whole 800,000-year range.

activities.caption: pair each fingerprint with what it proves
activities.name: ccFingerprintMatch

config.prompt: Fingerprints only enhanced greenhouse warming leaves — pair each with its reading:

pairs.left: the stratosphere cools while the surface warms
pairs.right: extra heat trapped below — a brighter sun would warm every layer instead

pairs.left: nights and winters warm faster than days and summers

pairs.right: fossil carbon is ancient and carries virtually none

config.why: Each fingerprint separates the human cause from the natural suspects — the sun's alibi is written in the vertical profile of the atmosphere itself.

activities.caption: call the slope — the accelerating cause
activities.name: ccSlopeEstimate

config.prompt: The Keeling curve's growth averaged about 0.8 ppm per year in the 1960s. Roughly how many ppm per year did it reach in the 2010s?
config.why: About 2.4 ppm per year — the slope steepens decade by decade, the signature of an accelerating cause, not a steady one.
config.context: The small annual zig-zag is the Northern Hemisphere's biosphere breathing: leaves take in CO₂ each boreal summer and release it each winter.

activities.caption: order the natural rhythms, longest first
activities.name: ccRhythmOrder

config.prompt: The natural drivers act on wildly different clocks — order them by timescale, longest first:
items: Pinatubo's sulphur aerosols — a year or two before raining out
config.why: From millennia down to a couple of years — none of these clocks can produce a 50% rise in CO₂ sustained over 170 years, and since about 1950 the natural forcings sum to roughly zero.

activities.anchor: Feedbacks are why a small push can shift a large system
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the greenhouse ledger
activities.name: ccGreenhouseCloze

config.text: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth about %%0%% K warmer than an airless world at our distance; livestock and flooded rice paddies emit methane, roughly %%1%% times stronger than CO₂ over 20 years; and the modern best estimate of warming per doubling of CO₂ is about %%2%% °C.
config.hint: One is what the energy-balance model shows when the greenhouse slider hits zero; one is per kilogramme over 20 years; one is the century-refined best estimate.

activities.caption: pin the rise — the ocean's slow thumb on the scale
activities.name: ccSeaPlace

config.prompt: Global mean sea level has been climbing since 1900. How far has it risen so far?
config.why: About 20 cm since 1900, now accelerating at 3.7–4.5 mm a year — roughly half thermal expansion so far, with the melt share the one that accelerates.

activities.caption: the council chamber — which lever do you pull?
activities.name: ccResponseBranch

config.root: You advise a coastal city council: the sea is climbing ~4 mm a year and summers are getting lethal. The budget covers one serious push this year.

start.text: Two levers are on the table. Which do you fund first?

choices.label: Cut the city's own emissions
choices.feedback: The long game — your tonnes help everywhere except, for decades, your own sea wall.

choices.label: Build for the water and heat already arriving
choices.feedback: Fast and local — but it cannot scale to unbounded warming.

choices.label: Fund neither fully — wait for the other to pay off first
choices.feedback: Sequencing is a choice too. Watch what it costs.

mitigation.text: Solar electricity fell about 90% in cost across the 2010s and wind is now the cheapest new power in much of the world; forests and wetlands can be restored as sinks, carbon can be priced. But this lever is global and slow — free-riding tempts everyone, and the sea keeps rising for decades regardless.

choices.label: Now add the local defences
choices.feedback: The practical follow-up — the two levers bind at different speeds.

adaptation.text: Sea walls and 'room for the river' where defended land is worth defending, managed retreat where it is not; drought-tolerant crops and drip irrigation; heat-action plans — Ahmedabad's saved hundreds of lives a year within a decade. But no wall adapts to 4 °C: this lever is local and fast, and stops there.

choices.label: Now work on the cause as well
choices.feedback: Back to the long game — adaptation cannot scale alone.

sequenced.text: Waiting on one lever while pulling neither is how decades are lost: mitigation delayed is mitigation compounded, because infrastructure built today locks in emissions for a lifetime.

config.why: Mitigation is global and slow; adaptation is local and fast — one without the other fails, which is why the syllabus asks you to evaluate them together, at every scale from diet to treaty.
